content: The Great Plague of Vienna occurred in 1679 in Vienna, Austria, which was the imperial residence of the Austrian Habsburg rulers. Based on contemporary accounts, the disease is believed to have been the bubonic plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. This bacterium was transmitted by fleas that were associated with black rats and other rodents. The epidemic devastated the city, which experienced recurring outbreaks into the early 1680s, resulting in the loss of an estimated 76,000 residents. Vienna, situated on the Danube River, was a significant trading hub connecting the East and West. Due to its position as a crossroads for trade, the city had suffered from periodic plague outbreaks since the first wave of the Black Death in the 14th century. The city was overcrowded and densely constructed, with descriptions indicating the absence of public sewer systems or drainage infrastructure. Streets were littered with foul-smelling piles of domestic waste. Additionally, warehouses storing trade goods such as clothing, carpets, and grain for extended periods were heavily infested with rats. The unsanitary and filthy conditions in Vienna were considered extreme, even for the time, and the plague was often referred to as the Viennese death in other parts of Europe. During the 1679 epidemic, a religious order known as the Brotherhood of the Holy Trinity established special hospitals for both children and adults. Although the nursing care provided in these hospitals was basic, it represented a significant improvement over other medical and public health measures available in the city. Physicians treated patients using methods such as emetics, bloodletting, and the application of noxious ointments. The bodies of plague victims were transported to the outskirts of the city and placed in large open pits for burning. However, these pits were left exposed to the open air for several days until they were nearly full, which allowed the infection to continue spreading among the rat population. To commemorate the city's survival from the Great Plague and subsequent outbreaks, the Viennese erected monuments, including the famous Baroque Karlskirche and the associated 69-foot plague columns known as the Pestsäule. The Great Plague of Vienna was part of a larger regional outbreak that affected Germany, Austria, Bohemia, and neighboring areas. This epidemic appears to have been introduced into the region from two opposing directions. It had been spreading in Western Europe for many years, traveling eastward along trade routes. The Great Plague of London (1664–1665), which is believed to have originated in the Netherlands during the 1650s, killed approximately 100,000 people and marked the first major epidemic in a series of outbreaks. In 1666, a severe plague struck Cologne and the Rhine region, persisting until 1670. The Netherlands experienced plague outbreaks from 1667 to 1669, but there are no definitive records of it after 1672. France saw its last plague epidemic in 1668. Between 1675 and 1684, a new wave of plague originated in the Ottoman Empire, encompassing Turkey and parts of the Balkans. This wave spread into North Africa, Bohemia, Poland, Hungary, Austria, and Saxony, generally moving northward. The island of Malta lost 11,000 people to the plague in 1675. The plague in Vienna in 1679 was particularly severe, causing at least 76,000 deaths. Other urban centers in the region experienced similar levels of mortality. For example, Prague lost 83,000 people to the plague in 1681. Dresden was affected in 1680, while Magdeburg and Halle experienced outbreaks in 1682. In Halle, 4,397 deaths were recorded out of a population of approximately 10,000. Many cities in northern Germany suffered during these years, but by 1683, the plague had disappeared from Germany until the epidemic of 1707. The Great Plague of 1679 also gave rise to the legend of Lieber Augustin (Dear Augustin). Augustin was a popular street musician who, according to the legend, fell into a pit containing the bodies of plague victims late at night while he was drunk. Remarkably, Augustin did not contract the disease, which may have been due to the protective effects of alcohol. He is remembered in the popular folk song Oh du lieber Augustin.
